title: The WebSocket Protocol

hero.subtitle: Enabling full-duplex, bidirectional communication over a single TCP connection, powering real-time web applications from chat to live data.

subtitle: Enabling full-duplex, bidirectional communication over a single TCP connection, powering real-time web applications from chat to live data.
summary: WebSocket gives a web page and a server a two-way channel over one TCP connection. It starts as an ordinary HTTP/1.1 request with an Upgrade header, and after the server answers 101 Switching Protocols both sides exchange small frames, either side at any time. Text, binary, ping, pong and close are all frame types.

tldr.problem: HTTP only lets the client ask and the server answer, so real-time pages had to poll or hold requests open.
tldr.mechanism: An HTTP Upgrade handshake turns the TCP connection into a framed, two-way channel, with each message carried in small frames with an opcode, length and a client-side mask.
tldr.outcome: Browsers and servers can push messages to each other at any time over one connection, with far less overhead than polling.

today: WebSocket is built into every major browser and is the transport under many chat, trading, gaming and collaboration apps. Libraries such as Socket.IO and many server frameworks wrap it. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 carry WebSocket through their own extended CONNECT mechanisms (RFC 8441 and RFC 9220), and WebTransport is a newer alternative for some uses.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
WebSocket provides a full-duplex communication channel over a single TCP connection. Unlike HTTP's request-response model, WebSocket allows both client and server to send messages independently at any time.

Before WebSocket, real-time web apps relied on inefficient techniques like long-polling or Comet. WebSocket provides a clean, efficient solution for bidirectional communication.
sections.plainLanguage: WebSocket provides a full-duplex channel over one TCP connection, so client and server can each send messages at any time. HTTP, by contrast, works as request and response. Before WebSocket, real-time web apps used less efficient techniques such as long-polling.

sections.title: Opening Handshake
sections.content:
WebSocket connections start as an HTTP/1.1 Upgrade request:

Client Request
GET /chat HTTP/1.1
Host: server.example.com
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13
Server Response
HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=

After this handshake, the connection transitions from HTTP to the WebSocket framing protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: A WebSocket connection begins as an HTTP/1.1 request with Upgrade: websocket and a random Sec-WebSocket-Key. The server replies 101 Switching Protocols with a matching Sec-WebSocket-Accept value. After that, the connection uses WebSocket framing instead of HTTP.

sections.title: Data Framing
sections.content:
WebSocket uses a lightweight frame-based protocol:

The figure shows the frame header for a client frame whose length needs the 16-bit extension. Each header field is listed with its exact width.
sections.plainLanguage: After the handshake, data travels in frames. Each frame has a small header with fields of exact widths, including a length, followed by the payload. The length field can be extended to 16 bits for larger frames.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
Chat Applications
Real-time messaging with instant delivery (Slack, Discord)
Live Data Feeds
Stock tickers, sports scores, IoT sensor data
Multiplayer Games
Low-latency game state synchronization
Collaborative Editing
Real-time document collaboration (Google Docs-style)
sections.plainLanguage: WebSocket suits applications that need fast two-way exchange. Examples are chat, live data feeds such as stock tickers or sensor readings, multiplayer games that need low-latency state updates, and real-time collaborative editing.

messages.label: 101 Switching Protocols
messages.note: Sec-WebSocket-Accept proves the server understood the handshake.

messages.label: Frame (text or binary)
messages.note: Either side can send at any time.

messages.label: Close frame
messages.note: The other side answers with its own Close, then TCP closes.

fields.name: FIN
fields.desc: Set to 1 on the final fragment of a message. The first fragment may also be the final one.

fields.name: RSV1
fields.desc: Must be 0 unless a negotiated extension defines it.

fields.name: RSV2
fields.desc: Must be 0 unless a negotiated extension defines it.

fields.name: RSV3
fields.desc: Must be 0 unless a negotiated extension defines it.

fields.name: Opcode
fields.desc: Frame type. 0x0 continuation, 0x1 text, 0x2 binary, 0x8 close, 0x9 ping, 0xA pong.

fields.name: MASK
fields.desc: 1 if the payload is masked. All client-to-server frames must be masked.

fields.name: Payload len
fields.desc: 0 to 125 is the length itself. 126 means a 16-bit length follows, 127 means a 64-bit length follows.

fields.name: Extended payload length
fields.desc: Present only if Payload len is 126 (16 bits). If it is 127 this field is 64 bits long.

fields.name: Masking key
fields.desc: Present only if MASK is 1. A 32-bit value used to XOR the payload data.
